title: The Day the Market Forgot How to Subtract

beats.text: In March two thousand, the market priced a profitable business below zero.
Imagine you own Three Com. It sells computer networks.
Inside it sits Palm, maker of the hottest handheld computer.
Three Com sells a sliver of Palm to the public.
Palm rockets from thirty-eight dollars to one sixty-five, then closes near ninety-five.
Each of your shares will get about one and a half Palm shares.
Over a hundred forty dollars of Palm. So your stock jumps?
So everything else Three Com owns is worth minus sixty-three a share.
How is a profitable business worth less than nothing?
You see, it's a wallet holding a hundred forty dollars, on sale for eighty.
Everyone saw it. Newspapers wrote about it.
But cashing in meant betting against Palm, and almost no Palm shares could be borrowed.
Everyone could do the math. Nobody could pick up the money.

facts.claim: On March 2, 2000 3Com sold a small part of Palm in an IPO and kept about 95 percent (sources give 4-6 percent sold)
Palm, maker of handheld computers; 3Com, profitable seller of computer network systems
Palm priced at $38, intraday high $165, closed $95.06 on day one
3Com shareholders were to receive about 1.5 Palm shares per 3Com share (1.525) in a later spin-off
1.5 x $95.06 = about $142.6 of Palm per 3Com share (arithmetic on two-source figures)
3Com fell from $104.13 to close at $81.81 that day
Implied stub value of 3Com's non-Palm assets: minus $63 per share, minus $22 billion in total
The mispricing was noted by the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times and persisted for months
Arbitrage was blocked by short-sale constraints: shorting Palm was very costly or impossible (short interest above 100 percent of float)

caption:
March 2000: 3Com owned about 95% of Palm, yet the market priced 3Com's own business at minus $22 billion.
Everyone could see it. Almost no one could profit from it, because Palm shares were nearly impossible to borrow.
